p: On January 11 Kit gave Boyd her routing slip for the pilot package. His block was the first of five, and for almost four weeks it sat in his inbox under his coffee cup.

On Tuesday nights she studied with Vern at his kitchen table on Cedar Street. He gave her one of his old navigator logs from 2001, with a young copilot named Lieutenant Merritt in it, and told her she'd get one a week and never the box.
When the slip had sat ten days, she shut Boyd's door and asked him straight what was holding it. He said give him till drill.

Corbin Haas told her he'd given the bars back after he washed out. He asked what happens to her if she washes out, and she said she'd come home and crew a jet, same as him. He said he wished he'd told somebody the truth sooner.

On the February drill Colonel Merritt stopped at two two eight and asked Kit why she wanted the slot, not why she deserved it. Kit gave her the wing's reasons, and Merritt said that wasn't what she'd asked.
On Sunday Boyd signed the slip without a word and put her name on every launch for the next three drill weekends.
Rae Sutter. Tech sergeant. A full time crew chief on the jet at the end of Kit's row.
Gene Albers. Kit's supervisor at the Tolliver water plant.
Rhonda Shaw. Kit's mother. She runs a school cafeteria across the river, and she's the only one who calls Kit Kitty.
According to the break room, Kit was already too old.

She heard it on Monday, February 8, at twenty to eight in the morning, with Boyd's signature folded in her chest pocket. The slip had four empty blocks left. The second one belonged to an office across the street from the hangar that didn't open until eight, so she'd come into the shop to kill twenty minutes with a cup she didn't want.

On weekdays the shop ran on the full timers. Boyd was on the phone in his office. Two of the young ones were arguing over a parts catalog at the counter. At the table by the window Tech Sergeant Rae Sutter was eating a breakfast burrito out of its foil. She'd crewed the jet at the end of the row since before Kit enlisted, and she knew everybody's business by the simple method of walking the line every morning and asking.
Sutter wiped her hands on a napkin and nodded at Kit's chest pocket, where the corner of the slip was showing. Word is you put in for the pilot slot.

Sutter looked at her the way you'd look at somebody about to step off a maintenance stand they thought was lower. Darrow. Somebody ought to tell you before you burn your whole spring on it. You have to be in pilot training before you turn thirty three. That's the rule. My cousin's kid missed it by four months. She folded the foil into a square. You're done, hon. I'm sorry.

The young ones had stopped arguing. Kit could feel the slip against her chest, and the work card behind it with five weeks on the back. She'd read the birthday line herself in January. But a posting was somebody's short version, and Sutter had walked this ramp since before Kit could drive. If the real rule said pilot training, and pilot training was a year out at best, then five weeks was a year and change. A year and change was a wall.

Thanks, Sergeant Sutter. I'm going to go read what it actually says before I quit on it. Sutter shrugged. Suit yourself. I'd want somebody to tell me. You did. At eight Kit walked the slip across the street and handed it over a counter, and she didn't let herself look back at the window.

Integrity and Professionalism. She did you a kindness, as she saw it, so you thanked her for that. You didn't take her word for the rule, and you didn't fight her in front of her airmen. Somebody tells you what a page says? Go read the page.
Tuesday, February 9, was her fifth Tuesday at the yellow table. She told Vern about the break room before she had her coat off, all of it, the cousin's kid included.
Vern asked what Sergeant Sutter had read. Kit said she didn't think Sutter had read anything. And you?

She had the copy the orderly room had printed for her in January, folded in thirds and worn at the creases from riding in her coat. She laid page one on the table. Vern put on his reading glasses and read it standing behind her chair, over her shoulder, the way she pictured him reading a chart over a pilot's.

Pilot vacancy, summer 2027 hiring board. The wing will select one applicant for undergraduate pilot training. The selection board convenes Saturday, July 10, 2027. Applicants must hold a bachelor's degree, meet commissioning standards, and have AFOQT scores on file by June 1, 2027. Minimum scores are on page two. Applicants must not have reached their 33rd birthday by the board date. Selection is contingent on a flight physical and on final approval above the wing.
Not Sutter's sentence. The paper's. Read me the birthday line to the period, and tell me which date it measures your age on.

July tenth. It says by the board date, and the board date's in the first line. Vern nodded. That's the paper's sentence. Sergeant Sutter has a different one. One of them is the short version. He reached for page two.
Page two had the minimum scores, in a box.

Pilot vacancy, page two. MINIMUM SCORES. AFOQT: Pilot 25. Verbal 15. Quantitative 10. CSO 10, with Pilot and CSO together 50 or higher. PCSM: 10 or higher, on file by the board date. ROUTING. Applications begin with the applicant's immediate supervisor.
Kit had read page two in January. She'd read the AFOQT line and stopped there. Vern's pencil went past it to the PCSM line and stayed.
That's your Pilot score, your TBAS and your flying hours, mixed by a formula nobody publishes. The TBAS is its own test, on a computer, with a stick. You'll need to book it.
I don't have any flying hours.

Then the other two carry it. He waited while she wrote TBAS on the back of page two. Then he turned back to page one and put the pencil under the last line. Selection is contingent on a flight physical and on final approval above the wing. Tell me what that says about the colonel's yes, and nothing it doesn't.

The wing picks. Then somebody above the wing says yes or no. Vern tapped the word contingent. She'd had that one in January too, out on the ramp, with Fisk asking what it meant and her not wanting to admit she had to think about it. And now? Depends on. He took the pencil off the page and didn't say anything else, which was about as close as Vern came to telling you you'd done fine.
Vern took his glasses off and folded them, which she'd learned meant he was about to say more than one sentence.

A posting is the short version. Somebody boiled a long rule down to a page so it would fit on a corkboard. When you asked me at the Riverside, I went and read the long one. Took me two Saturdays on the heritage room computer. He set the glasses on page one. It measures you on the date the posting names. Your board date. Sutter's sentence was the rule once, years back. It isn't now. And there's a door in it for somebody just outside the line. An exception to policy. You ask for it in your package, and the unit has to sponsor it.

The wing. The Lieutenant puts her name on it, then it goes up past her, and somebody up there says yes or no. I sat on this wing's boards for a lot of years. The number on that line has moved since my day. Every version I read had a door something like this one. He touched the five weeks she'd penciled in the margin. It's written for people a little outside. Five weeks is a little. Next summer you'd be a year and five weeks out, and nobody calls that a little.
You've known since January. You hadn't asked. He said it the way he'd said bring a pencil.

The wall had a crack in it after all, and a name on the crack. Kit thought of a line of block capitals in a log at home, LT MERRITT, COPILOT, and of the man across the table who'd written it. The thought got as far as her mouth.

She swallowed the other question. What does a request like that need in it? Vern looked at her a moment, as if he'd heard the one she hadn't asked too. A reason somebody can sign under. Your scores, when you have them. And your own words on why. He wrote all three down the margin of page one, one under the other.
And I don't call colonels, he said, to nobody in particular, getting up for the den.
He came back with one sheet out of the box and laid it down facing her.

My log, seven March, oh one. Tolliver to the track and home, five point eight hours. Weather going down at our alternate, so we picked a new one, a civil field, runway one seven, three five. The notice to airmen said that runway was closed oh four hundred to oh nine hundred Zulu, except with prior permission. The aircraft commander read closed and wanted another field. I read him the whole line. Called ahead and got permission. Didn't need it. Nice to have.

Except, Vern said. Most expensive word on any page, and people quit reading one word before it. He put his finger on the closure times. Tonight's question is easier. Zero four hundred Zulu. What's the Z doing on the end of it?

Universal time. One clock for everybody. Vern wanted to know when the runway had closed on a Tolliver kitchen clock, in early March, six hours behind. She did it on the margin. Ten at night, the evening before. He put the log on top of her posting, which she took to mean it was hers for the week.

The plant's shift huddle happened at a quarter to seven every morning in the control room, standing up, with the night shift half asleep and the day shift half awake. On Friday, February 12, Gene Albers had a new piece of paper.

Gene had run the Tolliver plant for twenty two years and liked his huddles short. He read the top of the notice out loud. State says we go to eight a month on the distribution samples, starting March. Less driving for whoever has the truck. He tacked it to the board by the door and went on to the filter backwash schedule.
Kit was nearest the board. She'd come off ten hours of night shift and was reading it before she'd decided to.

The state notice. Distribution chlorine residual samples, the minimum per month, effective March first. Rows by population served, then two columns, standard and reduced. Five hundred one to thirty three hundred people, four standard, two reduced. Thirty three hundred one to ten thousand, ten and four. Ten thousand one to twenty five thousand, twenty and eight. Twenty five thousand one to fifty thousand, thirty and twelve. The reduced column has an asterisk. A system may move to reduced monitoring only after the department approves it in writing. A system may apply after twelve consecutive months with no distribution sample below point two milligrams per liter free chlorine.
The sign out by the road said the plant served about eleven thousand eight hundred people. It had said so since the last census.

Finger on the third row, ten thousand one to twenty five thousand. Finger on the standard column. Twenty. She checked next door both ways, ten above and thirty below, and then the eight beside it, in the column Gene had read. Eight had a star on its heading.
Gene was still on backwash. Kit read the line under the table, the one the star pointed to, and then she read it again, slower.

Last August a main had broken on the east side, out past the grain elevator, and for one afternoon a dead end on Cooper Road had read 0.1 on the residual. Kit had pulled that sample herself, in the rain. It was in the log in her own handwriting.

Two things, in order. A year with nothing under 0.2, and then the state saying yes on paper. Tolliver's clean year couldn't even start until after Cooper Road, and nobody had asked the state for anything. Twenty a month, then, for months yet.
Gene got to the bottom of his list, looked around the room over his reading glasses, and asked what he asked every morning. Anything else?

Twelve people in the control room, half of them already reaching for coats. The day operator who had the truck this month was grinning about all the driving he wouldn't be doing. Gene stood by the door under his own notice, the way he'd stood under every notice for twenty two years. He was a good supervisor. On March 1 he was going to cut the plant's sampling by more than half, on account of a star he hadn't read.

She let the coats go on and the room empty, then took the notice off the board and knocked on Gene's open door. Gene. The reduced column has a star on it. She laid it on his desk with her thumb under the footnote. He read it, then read it again with his finger. He looked at the ceiling a while. Cooper Road. Last August. She nodded, and he picked up a pen. Twenty a month, then. I'll fix it at tomorrow's huddle myself. Where'd you get so particular about footnotes? Homework.

Communication, with some respect in it. The mistake was his, so he got to see it first and fix it himself, in front of the same people who'd heard it. You brought the page, not an opinion, and you pointed at the line. That's how you correct a boss: privately, early, with the evidence in your hand.
On Saturday morning Graham had the whiteboard off its bracket and flat on the kitchen table, with the week wiped clean.

He'd drawn twelve narrow columns across it in his lab quiz printing, one for every week from Monday the fifteenth through Sunday, May 9. In each column, in green, VERN, two hours on Tuesday. Then four one hour blocks in blue, wherever her plant shifts and his lab nights left a hole: two on weekdays, and one each on Saturday and Sunday morning. Over three of the columns he'd drawn his cartoon tanker, the drill weekends, and under each tanker he'd crossed out both weekend blocks. His own week was on there too, in black and smaller: his lab nights, and nothing else. The Saturday mornings that used to say HARDWARE STORE, or nothing, were blue now. Hers.
And the age thing? he said, still drawing.
There's a waiver. Vern says the wing has to sponsor it. The colonel.

Graham nodded at the marker. In the bottom corner he wrote MAY 15 with a question mark, the Saturday he'd picked, two weeks clear of June 1 in case the scores were slow. Past that the whiteboard just ended at its aluminum edge, and he didn't write anything there. She saw where the board stopped. She didn't ask what went on the other side of it, and he didn't say.
Pop quiz, he said, capping the green. No calculator. How many hours does that give you, from the fifteenth through the ninth?

Sixty six. Six a week is seventy two, and the three drill weeks lose two apiece. Graham wrote 66 under MAY 15 and drew a box around it, and then a second box around the first, which was how she knew he was pleased.

Seventy two less three times two. Or nine ordinary weeks at six, fifty four, plus three drill weeks at four, twelve. Sixty six either way. Pick the method you'll get right at minute twenty eight of twenty nine.

On Sunday, February 14, Kit drove across the river to her mother's. Rhonda had made a Valentine's supper every year since Kit was in kindergarten, pot roast and a heart shaped cake that never came out of the pan in one piece, and Graham was coming over once he'd finished grading.

The fridge in that kitchen had been collecting paper since before Kit could reach the handle. The family day picture was still on the freezer door, held up by a magnet from the dentist. Somebody had clipped February's lunch menu over the top half of it, so what showed was a seven year old in a seat too big for her, looking up at something hidden behind Tuesday's chili. Kit could have unclipped the menu. She knew what was under it, a hand pointing up, and she left it where it was, the same way she'd left the box on Vern's table alone.

Rhonda kept her back turned and her hands in the gravy. Darlene on my line says her nephew in the fuel shop says you're going to fly jets. And that you're too old, so you can't. Kitty, which is it, and why am I hearing it from Darlene?

You should've heard it from me. I'm sorry, Mom. Rhonda turned around then, spoon and all. So Kit told her: the board in July, her own birthday in June, the page that said board date where the break room said pilot training, and the door in the rule with the colonel's name on it. Not 2019. Her mother had 2019 the way the whole town had it, Boyd and his inspection, and Kit left that where it was too. Rhonda didn't interrupt once, which for her was close to a record. When it was done she pointed the spoon at her. So you're not too old. I'm too old unless. Rhonda put the spoon down on the stove and glanced at the freezer door, at the lunch menu. You were always looking up at something, Kitty.

Communication. The people close to you get it from you, first and straight, not secondhand off a cafeteria line. You owned that she found out the wrong way, and then you fixed the version she had. The test likes that order. Own the miss, then give the facts.
She'd written the letter of intent on Sunday night after supper and Monday at the plant, at the break table, between feed checks. The posting asked for one page. She'd made it fit.
On Tuesday, February 16, Vern read it with his pencil out. He didn't correct anything. He drew a small neat circle around two words, then around the same two words again further down, and kept going.

Letter of intent, first draft. I am applying for the wing's pilot training vacancy on the summer 2027 board. I have served in this wing for more than eleven years, and since 2018 I have been the dedicated crew chief on one of the wing's K C one thirty fives. In that time I have trained airmen for the wing and learned its aircraft from the ground up. The wing will convert to a new aircraft in the coming years. I believe the wing would be well served by a pilot who has crewed its jets and knows what it takes to launch them. As an officer I would continue to train airmen and support the wing's maintenance. My goal is to give back to the wing that has given me so much.
There was no shortage of I in it. I am applying, I have served, I believe. She'd checked. Each I was hauling a load for somebody else.
Vern slid it back across. Seven circles. Read it the way a board reads it, with twenty of these in a stack in front of them. One sentence. What's it about?

It's about the wing. Out loud it sounded worse than it had on paper. A pilot for the wing. Vern went down the circles with the tip of his pencil, tap, tap, tap, the whole page. Seven. Main idea's whatever a page keeps coming back to. Yours keeps coming back to us.
Vern took the letter back and turned it face down, so the circles were on the table and the words weren't.
It's a fine letter for the wing to write about you, Sergeant. The board can get that one from Boyd. So who's this one from?

I don't know how to write the other one. It was the truest thing she'd said at that table in five weeks of Tuesdays, and Vern, to his credit, didn't make a thing of it. Nobody does, the first time. Don't write the letter, then. Write me one sentence with you in it. Just the one. Bring it Tuesday.

On Saturday, February 20, Graham went to bed at ten with half a stack of chemistry quizzes still ungraded on the counter, and Kit stayed up with the laptop. She had Vern's copy out too, the one he'd circled. The twelve weeks were back up on the fridge in green and blue.

One sentence, Vern had said. Just the one. She left his circles alone and went to the bottom, to the line about giving back to the wing that had given her so much. She highlighted it and hit delete. Now the bottom of the page was empty except for the cursor, blinking where the sentence used to be.
For twenty minutes she typed things and took them back out. A couple were about the jet. One was about Boyd, and she got rid of that one fast. What stayed was four words.
Four words, on a page that had cost her two nights. She read them the way Vern had taught her, all the way to the period. Not one of them was carrying anything for anybody else.

The printer lived in the spare room on top of a box of Graham's old lab manuals. She got as far as the print window. Copies, 1. Under the floor the furnace kicked on, ran a while and quit, and she was still looking at the button.
She hit Cancel. She saved it as LETTER 2, right beside LETTER, and shut the laptop on both.
